blocks.t: Hey folks, I’m Matt Lowe, Design Director on THE FINALS, and in this blog update I want to discuss the results of our most recent Respec Order test, which ran from update 11.10 to 11.12.

Respec Order was a series of tests run during Seasons 10 and 11. For each Respec Order event, we rebalanced the game’s Light and Heavy archetypes in Cashout mode, giving Lights 25 more health and a slight movement speed reduction and giving Heavies 25 less health and a slight movement speed increase. Each test also included a handful of other balance changes.
For background, you can read about the original Respec Order test here, the results of that test here, and the results of Respec Order 2 here.
In this blog we’ll talk about the results of Respec Order 3, which concluded with the release of update 11.12, including the survey where we asked whether you’d like the changes made permanent.
But first, a reminder of why we’re testing Respec Order in the first place.
RESPEC ORDER | GOALS
The changes tested in Respec Order aim to address two common issues we see with the balancing of the game:

Movement Speed: We often see that the very wide range of archetype movement speeds in the game can cause teams to drift apart, making teamplay harder, especially for solo or more casual players. We wanted to test if bringing the movement speeds closer together could improve team cohesion by reducing this drift.

Health Scale: We know that extreme differences in health values in FPS games can make certain weapon types very hard to balance to feel good at both ends of the health scale (i.e., a gun feels equally good against Heavy and Light). We wanted to test if compressing that scale slightly can help make weapon balancing easier to do and if it can lead to better-feeling combat.
So how did those changes perform during Respec Order 3?
RESPEC ORDER | TEAM COHESION DATA
In Respec Order 3 we ran the same movement speed changes as the previous tests, making Lights slightly slower and Heavies slightly faster, to keep teammates closer together.
Just like in our previous tests, we analyzed these changes by measuring the distance between all members of the same team at key moments in a round, where we expected drift to be its worst:
10 seconds after initial spawns or team wipes
When a Vault is started by a team
When a Cashout is started by a team

At those points, we measured the distance between players A and B, B and C and C and A on the same team, giving us a score for approximate proximity. We then compared those data samples from the Respec Order test with Cashout in the game the two weeks before the test (our baseline). What we saw with this test is similar to the outcomes we got from previous tests. Teams with more Lights stayed closer together, with the distance between teammates down around 1% to 3%.
At the other end of the scale, teams with one or more Heavies tended to see a slight decrease in cohesion, around 0.5% to 1%, due to the increased Heavy movement speed.

An interesting outlier in this data was the triple Medium team composition, where cohesion seemed to drop 1.7%. We believe this change was unrelated to Respec Order 3 but actually a product of the Shockwave Specialization seeing increasing usage rates following the addition of a Glitch effect to it in 11.7. Usage climbed over several weeks and peaked during Respec Order 3. With the added mobility of Shockwave, some Medium-focused team compositions ended up drifting apart more often.
Cashout mode data for Shockwave pick rate among all archetypes.

This overall team cohesion data supports the benefits we saw from earlier tests. While the changes are not huge, there is a slight pull towards more coordinated teams with the changes to movement speed, and we see that as a positive for the game.
RESPEC ORDER | ARCHETYPE USAGE DATA

When it comes to analyzing the impact of both the movement and health changes on the different archetypes, there are many ways to measure it. Here we’ll focus on pick and win rates as a high-level measure of impact. We do look at metrics beyond these, but a blog covering every single measure we can check isn’t practical.
As with earlier Respec Order tests, the first thing we see in the most recent test is a shift in pick and win rates per archetype.

Heavy, our least-picked archetype, has had the highest win rate for a long time, but during the test that win rate comes down to around 52%. It’s worth noting here that a ‘win’ includes winning a final round, or finishing in the top two in a Cashout round. Medium stays largely in the same spot, with little change. The Light, which has had the lowest win rate for quite some time, sees a jump up in win rate from around 47.5% to 48.5%.
These may not seem like big changes, but in a game where ideally win rates would be close to 50%, win rates as high as 53% or as low as 47% are further from that than we’d like.

Another way to look at the changes is to see how they shift the different archetypes’ average kill and death rates per round, as both movement speed and health changes should change how effective the archetypes are in combat.

Again, we see the Medium barely move on this front. The Light, designed to be a ‘glass cannon’, did see a small shift up in kills and down in deaths, suggesting the loss of speed was more than offset by the increase in health. The Heavy, meanwhile, went in the opposite direction, getting slightly fewer kills and dying slightly more.

It’s worth pointing out here that while these movements in kill/death rate look large on the graph, they’re relatively small rate changes overall. For example, the average kills per round metric only varies from 4.6 to 4.95 per round across the whole scale, meaning archetypes are already quite close. It’s also fair to say that the Heavy’s kill rate up until now has been much higher than we originally designed for, so a leftwards shift here is something we see as a positive.

So generally, we see these results on the archetypes as being positive. They retain a unique position and role for each archetype, while bringing win rates much closer together, which is very important for the longevity of the game and the viability of each archetype.

Those results extend to team compositions. As the chart below shows, the pick rate for most team compositions essentially remained the same throughout the test, while all of the outlier win rates nudged closer to 50%. In the most extreme cases, HHM moved from a 55.86% win rate to 53.75%, while LLL moved from an awful 40.48% win rate to a slightly less awful 43%, so while these numbers are still not ideal, it’s a big step in the right direction.

For our design team, these are all positive results that shift the game towards a more balanced place while retaining the differences between the different archetypes, but how did you, our players, feel? On to the survey results!
RESPEC ORDER | PLAYER FEEDBACK

As with the previous Respec Order tests, we surveyed players in-game on how they felt about the changes. This time, we also asked players specifically if they would like the changes to be made a permanent addition to the game. Let’s go through the results.
Around 35% of eligible players completed the survey while it was active. This is not too dissimilar to what we saw in other tests.

Overall, 52.6% of players said yes, that they would like the Respec Order changes to be a permanent addition to the game. To better understand that result, it’s useful to break the results down across several dimensions.
The graph above shows how the approval rating varied across players based on the number of Cashout tournaments they had played in Season 11, prior to the survey.

The most hardcore players, those with over 100 tournaments played, had an approval rating of 45%. This was somewhat expected. For our most hardcore players, the game already has high appeal and they also frequently have very high win rates, so any change was likely to be somewhat negative for them.

For our core and more casual audience members, the majority of those surveyed, the approval rating for Respec Order varied from 50% to 62%. This was also somewhat expected, especially the higher rates among our more casual players. It’s an unwritten rule of FPS design that generally the closer health values are for different characters in a shooter, the more consistent weapons will feel and the more understandable combat encounters become, and we expected that better combat feel could be one outcome of Respec Order.

Looking at the survey results based on the respondent’s most recently used archetype, Heavy players averaged a 47% approval rate for the changes, while Mediums and Lights both averaged 55% approval rate. This was also somewhat anticipated: the health changes are the most noticeable part of Respec Order, and here the Heavy clearly loses out while Light gains. We suspect for Mediums combat in general just feels more consistent, which might impact the increased score there. Again it’s worth noting here that outside of Respec Order the Heavy has sustained the best win rate in the game for a very long time, so while they might feel they’re losing out in Respec Order, in reality the changes only bring their performance down to roughly where it should have been all along. One other vector by which we could view these results is by players’ skill rating.

As with tournament play rates above, the most active and most skilled players tended not to score Respec Order as highly, with the top tier bucket giving it a 43% approval rating. Players of average to lower skill ratings tended to approve, with ratings between 52% and 61%. Again, we feel this reflects a position of the more experienced and successful players being comfortable with the status quo that generally benefits them, while less frequent players are more open to changes.
Combining some of these metrics is also interesting. The matrix below sorts players both by tournaments played and skill rating, giving a more detailed breakdown of player sentiment.

For example, it becomes apparent that a small group of highly skilled players who played very little Cashout in Season 11 only approved the changes at a 44% rate, while a larger group of very engaged lower skilled players, having played 40+ tournaments in the season, approved at rates of 55% to 58%. This latter group are clearly still very engaged players, despite not necessarily being super highly skilled.

Overall though, approval for the Respec Order changes skews slightly to the positive side, with a 52.6% positive rating. This is largely in-line with the survey results we saw in previous Respec Order events, where we asked players to score the changes out of 5 and where the average response score hovered around 3 for each test.
RESPEC ORDER | WHAT’S NEXT?
So where does all of this leave us?

The data backs up that these changes have had a positive impact on gameplay overall. Teams are slightly more cohesive, matches result in slightly fairer outcomes, certain team compositions are more viable than before. For us as a developer, those are wins that improve the game.

We hear the concerns from some players that these changes erode the identity of each of the archetypes and we understand that argument, but we don’t fully agree. We believe far more of each archetype’s identity comes from their Specializations, Gadgets and Weapons. After all, is a Light really that fast without Evasive Dash or Grappling Hook? We don’t think so, and our stance is that archetype identity will remain intact as these changes go through.

Second, the survey results back up the idea that there is an appetite in the community for us to make these changes to the game. At a 52.6% approval rating there is a positive swing to the responses. Would we like that margin to be way clearer? Absolutely! The bigger the mandate, the more comfortable we can be making a change; when the sentiment is more divided it’s always a bit harder. In some ways, we could look at a 52.6% positive rating and view it as a situation where whatever we do, we’re going to annoy half our players anyway. Staying the same denies half the fanbase a change they would like, making the change risks alienating the other half.

In addition, with a survey completion rate of only around 35%, it could be argued that we’re not hearing from as many players as we should. While that is true, we’ve surveyed players on this topic on three different occasions now, seeing similar results each time. As a dev team, we take that to mean those who didn’t respond don’t feel strongly either way.

So, while it’s a tough choice, the sentiment and data come down in support of Respec Order being an improvement to the game and in Season 12 we will make the movement speed and health changes to Heavy and Light a permanent addition to the game.

As stated above, it’s not an obvious choice, and some players will definitely not like it, but for us the clinching factor outside of all the data and surveys is that we believe this will make the game better in the long run, and as a development team we have to do what we believe is best for our game. With the health difference between Light and Heavy dropping from 200 HP to 150 HP, we’ll have much more flexibility when it comes to balancing our weapons to feel good at both ends of the health spectrum. In turn, this should make the game easier to understand and make combat more consistent, and we believe that a better balance state for the game should help it retain new players and grow, and that’s something we all want.

These changes will go live along with one of the biggest balance patches we’ve ever done for the game. Given the scale of the changes, there are bound to be some things we get wrong that we’ll only see once the new meta settles in and thousands of players are playing the game, so between updates 12.0 and 12.3 we’re going to be especially active in reviewing the balance and making additional changes where we feel they are needed.

I want to thank all of you in the community for being involved in the Respec Order tests, providing feedback, comments and suggestions, and discussing the changes in addition to the survey. Your feedback has been invaluable in exploring these changes to the game and hopefully we can do more ‘experiments’ like this in the future, be it balance changes, items or modes, where your feedback can help shape the game. We look forward to seeing you all in the Arena for PRIME TIME!

blocks.t: Hi everyone,

This December, THE FINALS turns three. That's three years of cashouts, best-in-class destruction and unscripted moments that no one saw coming. The game has changed a lot in that time, and plenty of what's in it today started as feedback you provided, or something we noticed from watching how you actually play.
The next season arrives on October 20, and before we reveal everything that's in it, I want to talk about what this season means for the game and why we've approached it differently this year.

Normally we work on a season-to-season cadence. This year we planned differently. Rather than treat it as three separate efforts, we set one bigger goal across the whole year, focused on improving the game we already have and pushing further on the things that define THE FINALS.

That longer runway allowed us to take on work that doesn't fit inside a three-month cycle. With it we have been able to go deeper on existing parts of the game while also investing in larger, more complex systems that need more time to get right.
And while every season brings new content, the bulk of our energy went into deepening the experience as a whole. As we approach October, now is the time when much of that work comes together.
As we get closer to the launch of the season, I want to give you a glimpse of what it means, and share an updated roadmap!
PUTTING ON A BIGGER SHOW

Being a Contestant in the world's greatest game show has always been the heart of THE FINALS. Over the past few seasons, we've opened up more of the world around the game show, introducing players to characters like Dede and Jax, taking players through the Early Talent Program and bringing more stories into the game. In October we're taking that considerably further.

Sponsors are central to it. They've grown in importance season after season, and now we want them to be a core part of your experience as a Contestant. You're competing for someone, and we want that relationship to carry identity, personality and purpose, rather than being a passive progression system.

We're also strengthening the presentation of the game show itself. We’re reworking how Contestants, teams and Arenas are introduced, as well as how the show looks, feels and unfolds while you're playing.
BUILDING BETTER ARENAS

We've had almost three years of watching you play, fight and destroy your way through our Arenas, and it's taught us a great deal about what works and where we can do better. We can also do things now, technically, that weren't open to us when we built the first maps.

For the next season we're applying those lessons to the Arenas you already know, starting with the oldest ones. We've made significant updates to lighting and materials to improve visual quality and readability, and extensive level design changes to improve how they play. We also want each Arena to have a stronger identity, with its own sponsor, colors, and character.
The result is that the Arenas you know will look better, read more clearly, and play differently.
DESTRUCTION AND DYNAMISM

Destruction and dynamism are fundamental to THE FINALS, and dynamism is about more than destruction alone. Our ambition has always been Arenas where physics, materials and forces interact in ways that feel natural and predictable, giving you the freedom to experiment, improvise and find your own way through a fight.
In October we’re pushing that a lot further, with the most significant update destruction has had since launch.

Destruction is becoming more nuanced. Today a piece of the environment is mostly either intact or broken. With the updated system, parts of a structure can stay partly attached as they come apart; so floors sag, walls lean and buildings collapse in far more varied ways. A damaged floor might sag into the floor below, giving you a moment to react and leaving a new route between floors behind it. And when a larger structure collapses, the pieces it leaves behind can become new surfaces to move and fight across.

We're strengthening knock-on effects too, so one event can trigger another and set off chain reactions through the environment. And we're taking dynamism past destruction, with smoke that now responds to forces and changes in the Arena.

With far more happening between intact and destroyed, we've also worked on visual cues and consistency, so you can better understand what's going on, see what's coming and have time to do something about it.
We've rebuilt a lot of what destruction is made of as well, so a collapse carries far more weight and noise than it used to.
MORE SOON
Not everything we've worked on is something you'll see in a screenshot. Balance and performance have both had serious attention, and there's lots of work landing during this season on each of them.

We'll start sharing a lot more in the coming weeks and as we get closer to launch on October 20. We will also reveal a new Playstyle, a new Mode, a full UI and HUD rework, and so much more, so stay tuned!
For now, thank you for playing THE FINALS, and for your love of the game. None of this would be possible without you.
- Christian Aarsrud
Executive Producer
